grammar.note_en:
A topic is what a sentence is about. は follows that topic; as a particle it is read wa, although the ordinary kana is ha. In ゆいはかさをもちます, “Yui holds an umbrella,” ゆいは sets Yui as the topic. を (read o) follows the object: the thing being held or looked at. かさをもちます means “hold an umbrella”; ふだをみます means “look at a tag.” The verb comes at the end. Japanese does not need an English article a/the, and the noun does not change for English singular/plural. Here, follow the particular objects shown and named in the scene.

です gives a polite identification: れんのふだです means “It is Ren’s tag.” ではありません gives the corresponding negative: ゆいのかさではありません, “It is not Yui’s umbrella.” The story’s crucial contrast is between the owner of a tag and the owner of an umbrella. ゆいのふだです does not establish ゆいのかさです. Do not infer that every tag establishes the ownership of the object next to it. The small attached tag at the end is different from the loose card Yui is holding.

の connects a possessor or other associated noun to the following noun: れんのかさ is “Ren’s umbrella”; ほんのへや is “the room for books,” not “a room owned by a book.” The relation comes from context. Repeating names may help you initially; in natural conversation Japanese often omits a topic which is already clear. れんのほんです can mean “It is Ren’s book” without a separate word for it. Do not insert an English-style pronoun into every answer.

か marks a polite question. これはれんさんのふだですか means “Is this Ren’s tag?” これ means this thing, within the speaker’s immediate attention. さん follows another person’s name as a respectful suffix; speakers normally do not attach it to their own name. いいえ introduces a negative answer: “No.” A question can be answered with a complete identification instead of a separate yes. Yui’s reply いいえ、ゆいのかさではありません means “No, it is not Yui’s umbrella.” The affirmative question and full negative reply make her denial explicit.

だれ asks who; だれのかさですか is “Whose umbrella is it?” どれ asks which one; ゆいのほんはどれですか is “Which one is Yui’s book?” Give enough information to distinguish it, as in あかいほんです, “It is the red book.” あかい, あおい, おおきい and ちいさい precede the noun they describe: あかいほん, “a red book”; ちいさいふだ, “a small tag.” This chapter uses these complete forms, not their negative or past paradigms. ちがいます means “differ / be different”: ふだはちがいます, “The tags are different.” It does not mean every use of English wrong.

みます and もちます are polite nonpast forms. Here they describe the actions taking place in the scene, “looks at” and “holds.” The same form serves with Yui or Ren; there is no English third-person -s ending. Their dictionary forms and other conjugations will be taught later. どうぞ is the short offering “Here you are”; ありがとうございます means “Thank you.” The change in who holds each umbrella makes the handover clear without an additional transfer verb.

Keep kana distinctions when typing: あおい and あかい distinguish the umbrellas; おおきい has two initial お sounds, and ちいさい has a long い. Use your IME and consult How to read. Exercises A and B describe new small situations; use their cues rather than copy a story sentence. C asks what happened in this story and is self-checked: equivalent true sentences are acceptable. A subject or さん may be included or omitted where reference stays clear.
